title: Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs) in Plain Words
bigPicture: The IRS generally requires you to start taking money out of most retirement accounts at age 73. If you miss it, you owe a 25% tax on the amount you should have taken.
whatYouNeedToKnow: Required minimum distributions (RMDs) generally begin at age 73.
You can take your first RMD for the year you reach 73, or wait until April 1 of the following year. Waiting means you take two RMDs in that second year.
The tax on a missed RMD is 25% of the amount you should have taken. It drops to 10% if you correct the shortfall within two years. You report it on Form 5329.
Designated Roth accounts in employer plans, such as a Roth 401(k), do not have RMDs while the owner is alive. People who inherit them are subject to RMD rules.
If you are still working, you can usually delay RMDs from your current employer's plan until you retire, unless you own 5% or more of the business. This does not apply to IRAs.
Most people use the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table to figure the amount.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Guessing the amount instead of using the IRS table or your plan provider's calculator.
Assuming still working means no RMDs on an IRA. The still-working delay applies only to your current employer's plan.
Missing the deadline and owing the 25% tax.
actionSteps: Check the IRS RMD page below for the rules that apply to you and your birth year.
Ask your plan provider whether they will calculate your RMD.
Use the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table or a calculator to figure the amount.
Note your deadline on a calendar.
Ask a tax professional to review your plan before your first RMD year.
